strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for researchers in program representation learning and software analysis. Transferring information from source code and generated comments into low-level code representations has an identifiable interested audience.

The evaluation spans four downstream tasks. Reported improvements are promising: function-name accuracy reaches 33.41% versus 29.41% for the strongest reported baseline, and summarization BLEU-4 reaches 34.36 versus GraphCodeBERT’s 32.43.

The overall training pipeline is understandable, and the primary-contrastive variant plus comment and anchor ablations provide useful initial diagnostics. A carefully supported account of these findings would be valuable under TMLR’s criteria without requiring state-of-the-art performance.
weaknesses: Necessary: Align the binary-analysis claims with the evaluated inputs. Sections 3.1–3.2 generate LLVM IR directly from source, while Figures 7–8 retain informative function and callee names. This does not establish effectiveness on stripped executables or IR recovered from them. The first-page assertion that these representations are trivially interchangeable is inaccurate. Either evaluate the claimed deployment setting or narrow the scope to the compiler-generated LLVM representations actually studied, documenting retained symbols and metadata.

Necessary: Resolve the POJ-104 evaluation contradiction. Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify nonoverlapping training/development/test problem labels, with 64/16/24 classes, but Section 4.2 describes classification into 104 classes and reports metrics across all 104. Conventional supervised classification cannot learn the identities of classes absent from training. If this is actually retrieval, specify the training objective, candidate pool, relevance definition, and metric calculations. This ambiguity also affects Table 7’s ablations. For AnghaBench, clarify model selection and split boundaries, since Section 3.2 reports generation performance on the validation set.

Necessary: Specify the executable method more completely. Encoder checkpoints and initialization, tokenization and pooling, projection/interpolation network dimensions, and downstream generation decoders are insufficiently described. Equation 4 omits the softmax stated in the prose, leaving unnormalized similarities as cross-entropy targets; normalization and gradient flow through those targets need clarification. Also reconcile randomly selecting any two modalities with freezing both source/comment encodings, since selecting those two alone would not update the binary encoder.

Necessary: Strengthen or narrow the attribution to interpolation and gradual learning. PCL receives 10 pretraining epochs, whereas the full model receives 30 or 70. The assertion that PCL converged is unsupported by learning curves, and the experiments do not separately identify the benefits of scalar interpolation, feature-wise interpolation, and their ordering. Comparable training budgets and targeted controls would support the component claims; otherwise, report the result as a comparison between complete training configurations.

Necessary: Calibrate the superiority claims to the evidence. Results use single seeds without uncertainty estimates, and reverse-engineering performance is mixed: GraphCodeBERT has higher BLEU-4, while CONTRABIN’s exact-match advantage is only 0.43 percentage points. Large relative improvements over RoBERTa also obscure smaller gains over stronger baselines. Report uncertainty where needed to establish these differences, or describe them as tentative. Broad state-of-the-art claims should be limited to the evaluated comparators.

Necessary: Separate lexical agreement from semantic correctness. Summarization relies on CodeT5-generated comments, and reverse engineering is assessed through text-overlap metrics and selected examples, without compilation, execution, or systematic human assessment. These measurements do not establish the claimed semantic consistency or human comprehension benefits. Figure 7 even presents GraphCodeBERT’s semantically equivalent 'Unloads the mutex' alongside CONTRABIN’s 'Unloads a mutex,' weakening the claimed qualitative distinction. Add appropriate semantic validation or restrict conclusions to reference-text agreement.

Necessary: Correct the embedding-analysis interpretation in Section 4.1. Unique programs can share semantic structure and legitimately cluster. Cluster counts and distances in separately fitted t-SNE plots do not prove better representation quality. Remove these deductions or replace them with quantitative evaluation tied to a defined semantic relation.

Optional: Shorten the speculative human-learning analogy and correct inconsistent dataset names, GLUE/GLEU terminology, task counts, and figure/table references. These changes would improve readability, although the evidence and protocol issues above determine my recommendation.
